Reference data

Source: vignettes/reference-data.Rmd
reference-data.Rmd

Eight of the tests compare a record with reference data from a shipped layer: points (capitals, country and province centroids, biodiversity institutions, artificial hotspots) and polygons (land, urban areas, countries). The ninth, range, needs species range polygons, which the user supplies (see the article on custom gazetteers). This article lists where each layer comes from, how the package’s own gazetteers compare with CoordinateCleaner’s, how much the choice of land scale changes the sea test, and how the reference version is recorded with the flags.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/OccurrenceCleaner")

Needs a C++ compiler (Rtools on Windows).

library(OccurrenceCleaner)

The layers 

ri <- reference_info()
knitr::kable(ri[, c("layer", "source", "file", "version", "retrieved")])
layer source file version retrieved
land_110 Natural Earth ne_110m_land.zip 4.1.0 2026-10-09
land_50 Natural Earth ne_50m_land.zip 4.1.0 2026-10-09
land_10 Natural Earth ne_10m_land.zip 5.1.1 2026-10-09
countries_50 Natural Earth ne_50m_admin_0_countries.zip 5.1.1 2026-10-09
urban_50 Natural Earth ne_50m_urban_areas.zip 4.1.0 2026-10-09
places_10 Natural Earth ne_10m_populated_places_simple.zip 5.1.2 2026-10-09
admin0_10 Natural Earth ne_10m_admin_0_countries.zip 5.1.1 2026-10-09
admin1_10 Natural Earth ne_10m_admin_1_states_provinces.zip 5.1.1 2026-10-09
institutions GBIF GRSciColl grscicoll_institutions.tsv 2026-10-09 2026-10-09
aohi Park et al. 2023, AHOI (Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.v41ns1s0p) birds_20221010.csv, insects_20221010.csv, mammals_20221010.csv, plants_20221010.csv 2022-10-10 2026-10-10

Each row also holds the download URL, the SHA-256 checksum of the source file and the licence. The tests read these layers:

test reference data
capital Natural Earth populated places: admin-0 capitals, alternative capitals and capitals of dependent territories
centroid Natural Earth admin-0 country centroids and label points, admin-1 label points
institution GBIF GRSciColl institutions with coordinates
gbif_headquarters one fixed point, 12.58 E, 55.67 N
aohi Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (Park et al. 2023), 308 points
sea Natural Earth land at 1:110m (default), 1:50m or 1:10m
urban Natural Earth urban areas 1:50m
country_mismatch Natural Earth admin-0 countries 1:50m

All Natural Earth layers are in the public domain; the Natural Earth terms of use say that “No permission is needed to use Natural Earth.” The institutions come from the bulk export of GBIF’s Global Registry of Scientific Collections (GRSciColl), retrieved on 2026-10-09: 10,002 institutions, of which 6,085 have coordinates. The five of these that the zero test would flag are left out: four are registered within 0.14 degrees of (0, 0), although they are in Portugal, Nigeria, Turkey and Taiwan, and one has a longitude of exactly 0. Kept, they would mark every record at (0, 0) as lying at an institution as well. GRSciColl absorbed the Global Registry of Biodiversity Repositories (GRBio) in 2018 and is synchronised weekly with Index Herbariorum. GBIF publishes the registry through its open API and states no separate licence for it.

The Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (AHOI) of Park, Xie, Thammavong, Tulaiha and Feng (2023) lists the coordinates that recur most often in GBIF records of plants, birds, insects and mammals, with the reason each recurs: 154 plant, 51 bird, 51 insect and 52 mammal points. It is built from the authors’ deposit on Dryad (doi:10.5061/dryad.v41ns1s0p), released under CC0, and keeps 308 points with coordinates. CoordinateCleaner’s bundled aohi table has 309; the two share 303 points, and the others differ in a few bird points and one plant coordinate (42.26 N there, 42.20 N in the deposit).

The layers are rebuilt from the sources CoordinateCleaner itself draws on, by the scripts in data-raw/ of the source repository; CoordinateCleaner’s code and data are GPL-3, and nothing is copied from them.

How the gazetteers differ from CoordinateCleaner’s

The package gazetteers describe the same places as CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1’s countryref and institutions tables, but they are not the same tables. Measured on 2026-10-09:

gazetteer CoordinateCleaner OccurrenceCleaner
capitals 225 (one per ISO3 code) 243 (215 admin-0 capitals and alternative capitals, plus dependent-territory capitals)
country centroids 660 rows from the CIA World Factbook, thematicmapping.org and geo-locate 516 (polygon centroid and label point per country, Natural Earth 5.1.1)
province centroids 4,645 (older Natural Earth admin-1 label points) 4,596 (Natural Earth 5.1.1 admin-1 label points)
institutions 9,773 with coordinates (GRBio, Index Herbariorum, GBIF, BGCI, Wikipedia, GeoNames) 6,080 (GRSciColl, without the five at zero coordinates)

  • Capitals. 212 countries match by ISO3 code. The median distance between the two packages’ capital points for the same country is 0.92 km, 90 % are within 7.1 km; CoordinateCleaner’s coordinates are rounded to 0.01 degrees. Natural Earth also lists alternative and official capitals that CoordinateCleaner does not hold: Cape Town and Bloemfontein besides Pretoria, Sucre besides La Paz, Naypyidaw instead of Yangon, Dodoma instead of Dar es Salaam, among others.

  • Country centroids. The two define centroids differently, so the points lie a median of 30 km apart (90 % within 259 km). Both use a 1 km buffer, so they flag different records: each catches records georeferenced to its own definition of the centre of a country.

  • Province centroids. CoordinateCleaner’s province centroids are exactly the Natural Earth admin-1 label points of an older release: all 4,549 codes that still exist match at distance 0. The package uses the 5.1.1 release, in which 96 of CoordinateCleaner’s codes no longer exist.

  • Institutions. The package uses GRSciColl only. CoordinateCleaner’s table also has 712 botanic gardens from Botanic Gardens Conservation International, 627 points from Wikipedia and 3 from GeoNames, which are not rebuilt here. GRSciColl has added institutions since CoordinateCleaner’s table was compiled.

The capital difference shows directly in the flags. Records at a few alternative or official capitals, under both references:

x <- data.frame(city = c("Pretoria", "Cape Town", "La Paz", "Sucre", "Yangon", "Naypyidaw"),
                species = "a",
                decimalLongitude = c(28.19, 18.42, -68.15, -65.26, 96.16, 96.13),
                decimalLatitude = c(-25.75, -33.92, -16.50, -19.04, 16.80, 19.75))
data.frame(city = x$city,
           natural_earth = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital,
           CoordinateCleaner = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner")$flag_capital)
#>        city natural_earth CoordinateCleaner
#> 1  Pretoria          TRUE              TRUE
#> 2 Cape Town          TRUE             FALSE
#> 3    La Paz          TRUE              TRUE
#> 4     Sucre          TRUE             FALSE
#> 5    Yangon          TRUE              TRUE
#> 6 Naypyidaw          TRUE             FALSE

Cape Town, Sucre and Naypyidaw are flagged only with the Natural Earth list; Pretoria, La Paz and Yangon under both. Which list is right depends on what an error looks like: a herbarium sheet in Cape Town georeferenced to the city is as wrong under either reference, and only the Natural Earth list catches it.

Land scale and the sea test

The sea test flags records outside the land polygons. The coarse 1:110m layer, the default of CoordinateCleaner’s cc_sea() (its clean_coordinates() uses 1:50m), smooths the coast and drops small islands; the 1:50m layer follows the coast more closely. A grid of points over Denmark and the western Baltic shows where the two disagree:

g <- expand.grid(decimalLongitude = seq(7.5, 15.5, by = 0.05),
                 decimalLatitude = seq(54, 58, by = 0.05))
g$species <- "a"
s110 <- flag_occurrences(g, tests = "sea")$flag_sea
s50 <- flag_occurrences(g, tests = "sea", land_scale = 50)$flag_sea
g$verdict <- ifelse(s110 & s50, "sea at both", ifelse(!s110 & !s50, "land at both",
                    ifelse(s110, "sea at 1:110m only", "sea at 1:50m only")))
table(g$verdict)
#> 
#>       land at both sea at 1:110m only  sea at 1:50m only        sea at both 
#>               5765                519                783               5974
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(g, aes(decimalLongitude, decimalLatitude, fill = verdict)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`land at both` = "#C8B88A", `sea at both` = "#A9C7E0",
                               `sea at 1:110m only` = "#C0392B", `sea at 1:50m only` = "#2C3E50")) +
  coord_quickmap(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "longitude", y = "latitude", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA))

On this grid the two scales disagree for 10 % of the points, all of them along the coast. At 1:110m Funen, Lolland, Falster, Rügen and Bornholm are missing, so records on them are flagged as at sea (red); the coarse 1:110m coastline also reaches out into the water, so records in a strip of coastal water count as on land there and are flagged only at 1:50m (dark). For coastal and island taxa the scale therefore changes a share of the sea flags large enough to see in a tally. The 1:10m layer is the most detailed of the three and is downloaded on first use:

download_reference("land_10")
f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "sea", land_scale = 10)

The download is checked against the SHA-256 in reference_info() and refused if Natural Earth has published a different file under the same name. The converted layer is stored in tools::R_user_dir("OccurrenceCleaner", "cache"), so it is downloaded once per machine.

Buffers

The buffers are the other half of every proximity test. They default to CoordinateCleaner’s (10 km for capitals, 1 km for centroids and the GBIF headquarters, 100 m for institutions, 0.5 degrees around (0, 0)) and are changed per test:

x <- data.frame(species = "a", decimalLongitude = c(16.37, 16.45), decimalLatitude = c(48.21, 48.21))
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital
#> [1] TRUE TRUE
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital", buffers = list(capital = 2000))$flag_capital
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE

A buffer of 2 km for capitals keeps records from the outer districts of a capital while still removing those placed at the city’s coordinates. The 0.5-degree zero buffer is in degrees, the others in metres.

Recording the reference

Every flagged data frame carries the reference that produced it, with the version of each layer:

f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("capital", "sea"), land_scale = 50)
attr(f, "occ_reference")
#> [1] "natural_earth (land 50; land_110 4.1.0, land_50 4.1.0, land_10 5.1.1, countries_50 5.1.1, urban_50 4.1.0, places_10 5.1.2, admin0_10 5.1.1, admin1_10 5.1.1, institutions 2026-10-09, aohi 2022-10-10)"
attr(f, "occ_layout_version")
#> [1] 3

reference = "CoordinateCleaner" stamps the installed CoordinateCleaner version instead. For streamed input the same label is written to the output directory, and a rerun into that directory with a different reference, land scale, set of tests or layout stops with an error, so one output directory never mixes flags from two references.

Choosing a reference

  • reference = "natural_earth" (the default) needs no other package, has a version and checksum for every layer, and uses current Natural Earth and GRSciColl data.

  • reference = "CoordinateCleaner" gives CoordinateCleaner’s flags up to the differences listed in the article Coming from CoordinateCleaner, for example to compare with a published analysis that used it. It needs CoordinateCleaner installed, and rnaturalearth for the polygon tests, which downloads the Natural Earth layers at run time as CoordinateCleaner does.

Both references use the same buffers and the same geodesic distance, so the difference between them is in the points and polygons only.
